title: The Value Puzzle
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart names and frames what he calls the "Value Puzzle": the gap between students' widespread, often bleak experience of school (citing a pre-COVID survey finding 75% of secondary students experience school as a form of misery) and his own conviction that mastery of academic disciplines is inherently and lastingly good. Using the Stockdale Paradox framing from a previous piece, he treats students' negative experience as the "brutal facts" that must be confronted honestly, while holding an "unwavering faith" that classes are genuinely valuable and can be experienced as good. The piece functions as a table-setting introduction to a planned series, previewing two solution paths -- teacher-led Mini-Sermons (already covered) and student-generated Valued Within exercises (to follow) -- without fully unpacking either yet.
points: Stuart anchors the piece in survey data (75% of secondary students report experiencing school as a form of misery) rather than treating the "kids don't value school" problem as anecdotal.

He explicitly imports the Stockdale Paradox structure from a previous article, using "brutal facts" (misery) and "unwavering faith" (inherent value) as the two poles teachers must hold simultaneously.

His negative-example list ("I learned too much," "I'm annoyed I became so good at math") makes vivid the counterintuitive claim that no one regrets mastering a discipline, however they may feel about school in the moment.
The piece is structured as a deliberate series opener, previewing Mini-Sermons and Valued Within exercises as the two complementary solution paths to the puzzle it names.
quotes: The vast majority of students today have a deeply impoverished view of the value of an education. It's way more popular today to decry the pointlessness of learning school subjects than it is to Value them.
A pre-COVID national survey found that 75% of secondary students experience school as a form of misery. In Stockdale Paradox language, these are the brutal facts.
What school offers is straightforward, though often obfuscated: We promote the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them toward mastery of the disciplines.

I've yet to meet a person who looks back on their schooling and says things like: "Darn it — I learned too much." "I'm annoyed that I became so good at math." "I wish I hadn't learned all that science.

On the brutal facts side, most students don't think school is inherently valuable and don't experience school as a good thing. On the unwavering faith side, all of the classes we teach ARE inherently valuable and CAN BE experienced as good.
